```{r}
#2
#Both read_csv() and read_tsv() share several common arguments that help in reading and processing data efficiently. These include col_names to specify column names, col_types to define data types, and na to identify missing values. Additionally, they support trim_ws to remove extra whitespace, n_max to limit the number of rows read, and guess_max to control the number of rows used for guessing column types.

```

```{r}
# 3
#The read_fwf() function, used for reading fixed-width files, has three key arguments that help define the structure of the data. fwf_widths() allows manual specification of column widths, while fwf_positions() defines exact column positions. Additionally, col_types is used to specify the data types of each column, ensuring accurate parsing of the file.

```

```{r}
library(readr)

read_csv("x,y\n1,'a,b'", quote = "'")


```

```{r}
#Mismatch → The first row has two columns, but the following rows have three; correct it as read_csv("a,b,c\n1,2,3\n4,5,6").

```

```{r}
# Load tibble package
library(tibble)

# Create the tibble with non-syntactic names
annoying <- tibble(
  `1` = 1:10,
  `2` = `1` * 2 + rnorm(length(`1`))
)

# Extract the variable called `1`
annoying$`1`

# Plot `1` vs `2`
plot(annoying$`1`, annoying$`2`)

# Create a new column `3`, which is `2` divided by `1`
annoying <- annoying %>%
  mutate(`3` = `2` / `1`)

# Rename columns to one, two, and three
annoying <- annoying %>%
  rename(one = `1`, two = `2`, three = `3`)


```
